These parallel fields include the burgeoning ODT industry; previous study and adoption of ATN systems, particularly as it applies to the design and operation of resilient, high-capacity stations; the automated people mover system industry and its reliance on infrastructure intelligence to augment system safety; and electric vehicle (EV) powertrains and their associated charging infrastructure and impacts on fleet operations. Phase III research into AMDs spans approximately 2022 through early 2025. Although Phase III continued to monitor the initial early-stage deployments, most Phase III research was a product of the intersection of the parallel fields described previously and the operational requirements of an AMD network system. This summary provides an overview of the research from Phase III organized into the following topical areas: • Impacts and implications of the on-demand network service mode • Management systems integrated into the operational control of the AV fleets • Battery electric fleet vehicle charging infrastructure • Boarding station/curbfront configuration and infrastructure • Systems engineering methodology for planning, analysis, and management of AMDs. Although organized into these stand-alone topics, many interconnections and interdependencies exist. The convergence of transportation system automation, electrification, and expectation for on-demand service for future mobility within urban areas is increasingly evident as AMD technology progresses. Although powertrain electrification was not uncommon in the 10 early deployment sites, the impacts of a fully electrified vehicle powertrain on AV fleet operations was not a central focus of research until now. With the growth, maturation, and steady adoption of EV technology, combined with early AMDs beginning to scale from a handful of vehicles to larger fleets, an initial investigation of operational consequences of EV powertrains is warranted. Similarly, the rapid adoption of commercial ride-hailing services in the 2010s and the burgeoning ODT market that has emerged since the COVID-19 pandemic both point toward the growing expectation for AV fleets to provide on-demand mobility service for community/district circulation and FMLM connectivity to regional and interregional transportation modes. As the timeline for AMD implementation becomes clearer, with the first prototypical district- scale deployment sites expected to be delivered in the next 5 years, NLR’s Phase III studies have focused on the operational implications for the convergence of 1) electrification of the many light-duty fleets deployed with BEV propulsion systems and 2) automation of operational fleets for moving people and goods—all within the context of the proliferation of on-demand passenger and goods movement (Lott and Young 2023).
